title: Napoleon Faces the Royal Troops at Laffrey
text:
In February 1815 Napoleon escaped from exile on the island of Elba and landed in southern France with about a thousand men. He marched north through the Alps toward Grenoble, avoiding the main roads where royalist troops waited.

On March 7, near the village of Laffrey, his way was blocked by a battalion of the 5th Line Infantry Regiment, sent by the royalist government to stop him. Their muskets were loaded. Napoleon's small force could not have fought its way through, and a single volley could have ended his return.

According to accounts of the scene, Napoleon ordered his own men to lower their weapons and walked forward alone toward the soldiers, wearing his familiar gray greatcoat. Within range, he stopped, and called out to the soldiers of the 5th that he was their emperor. He opened his coat and said that if any of them wanted to kill his emperor, here he was.

The soldiers did not fire. They broke ranks, shouting "Vive l'Empereur!", and went over to him. Regiment after regiment followed. On March 20 Napoleon entered Paris without a battle. The Hundred Days ended at Waterloo in June.
lesson: Facing people directly, and openly accepting the risk, can win them over when force or argument would fail.
source: Contemporary accounts of the Return from Elba, including memoirs of officers present
caveat: The exact words Napoleon used vary between accounts.
